item.description: No one can rival OpenAI for internal drama. But in recent days, Meta Platforms seems to be trying its best to do so. Earlier this week, Wired reported that Chief Technology Officer Andrew Bosworth told staff Meta had done an "atrocious" job of launching a new AI division. That report followed another one in Wired about the internal dissatisfaction within the company's applied AI division, citing Chief Product Officer Chris Cox acknowledging the "insanity of this company" (more on that issue). item.title: A Competitor to OpenClaw Emerges
item.description: After the success of OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent software that took the tech world by storm earlier this year, it's no surprise that copycats are popping up. And some of these copycats are catching up to OpenClaw, by some measures. Hermes, an agent tool from Nous Research, recently eclipsed OpenClaw in terms of new GitHub contributors in the last 30 days, according to GitHub data compiled by ClawCharts, which tracks the growth of open-source AI agents. (New GitHub contributors are a measure of how strong developer engagement is). And if OpenClaw continues to struggle with evolving from an experimental hacker project to a reliable piece of software, as we've written about here, Hermes and other alternatives like Nvidia's NemoClaw or Genspark Claw would have a bigger opening to break through. Hermes, like OpenClaw, is AI agent software that runs locally on users' devices. It can be used to automate any task you might complete on your computer, like writing code, searching the web for a rare vintage item or sending emails or WhatsApp messages. Nous Research says that what makes Hermes different from OpenClaw is that the agent can teach itself over time how to do the tasks its user asks it to do most often. Hermes does this by automatically writing "skills," or a manual of sorts that tells an agent how to do a task. It writes up these instructions automatically when, for instance, it completes a complex task that requires more than five "tool calls" (such as searching the web or accessing apps like Gmail or Discord) or when it finds a working solution after hitting a bunch of dead ends. (Nous has raised $70 million since its founding in 2023 from investors including Paradigm, OSS Capital and Distributed Global).

item.title: Manus' Revenue Soars as Original Investors Move to Reverse Meta Deal
item.description: The early Chinese backers of AI firm Manus are planning to buy the firm back from Meta Platforms at the $2 billion price Meta paid, in response to a Chinese government order that the deal be reversed, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. While the government's order has sparked alarm among Chinese startup founders, seemingly cutting off the U.S. as an avenue for fundraising or sale, reversal of the sale holds a bright spot for Manus' original investors. That's because Manus has continued to grow dramatically since the U.S. tech giant swallowed it up, according to the people.

Shazeer left Google in 2021 to co-found a chatbot startup Character.AI, but rejoined Google's AI team DeepMind in 2024 as part of a $2.7 billion deal with his AI startup. item.title: Building an early warning system for LLM-aided biological threat creation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]

This work serves as an initial step for ongoing research and discussions within the community.

item.description: gpt-oss-safeguard-120b and gpt-oss-safeguard-20b are two open-weight reasoning models post-trained from the gpt-oss models and trained to reason from a provided policy in order to label content under that policy.
